bib.title: Objective Bayes Inference and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Computer Age Statistical Inference, ch. 13)

question: How can Bayesian inference be made objective (uninformative priors, BIC) and computable (Gibbs sampling, MCMC), and what are the costs?
contributions: Surveys flat, Jeffreys, coverage-matching and conjugate priors
Shows BIC versus Fisher's scale contradiction via sample-size coherency
Explains Gibbs sampling and Metropolis-Hastings MCMC with vasoconstriction and population-admixture examples

results.claim: Objective priors dominate applied Bayes: 8 of 24 articles in one journal issue used Bayesian analysis, mostly objective priors
results.source: Efron and Hastie count of AoAS Dec 2014
results.setup: Annals of Applied Statistics, December 2014 issue
results.quote: Annals of Applied Statistics, 8 employed Bayesian analysis, predominantly

results.claim: Flat-prior posterior for Poisson x=10 is shifted about 0.5 right of the confidence density; Jeffreys prior 1/sqrt(theta) nearly matches it
results.quote: is shifted almost exactly 0.5 units right

results.claim: BIC Bayes factor for vasoconstriction slope test is 5.49, positive but not strong on Jeffreys' scale, while z=2.36 is between substantial and strong on Fisher's scale
results.setup: Logistic regression, n=39, M0: alpha1=0, d=1, W=7.07
results.quote: positive but not strong evidence against M0
results.note: Text layer prints numbers as 7:07 and 5:49; value from text 'W D 7:07'. Wilks W=7.07, z=2.36, coverage 0.982

results.claim: BIC and Fisher's scale give contradictory verdicts at large n: z=3.29 (p=0.001) is overwhelming on Fisher's scale but barely worthwhile on Jeffreys'
results.setup: One extra covariate, d=1, z=3.29, n=10,000 (Table 13.5 last column)

results.claim: Probability BIC-type criterion selects M1 under M0 with W>=2cn: 0.157 for AIC (cn=1), 0.0024 for BIC at n=10,000; cn=1.92 gives 0.05
results.quote: This equals 0.157 for the AIC choice cn

results.claim: 95% confidence interval for the effect at z=3.29, n=10,000 is (0.013, 0.053), a small effect BIC calls uninteresting
results.setup: Model M1 normal mean, z=3.29, n=10,000; lower bound 0.013 (sign unconfirmed for any minus signs)

results.claim: On prostate histogram, AIC, BIC (n=49), BIC (n=6033) and GIC (cn=1.92) all pick the degree-4 log-polynomial model
results.setup: N=6033 genes, 49 bins width 0.2, Poisson regression, degrees 2 to 8
results.quote: fourth-degree polynomial model was the winner

results.claim: Gibbs-sampled Bayesian t-test gives Pr(delta<0)=0.0028 versus frequentist one-sided p=0.0047
results.setup: Vasoconstriction data, y=1 (n=20) vs y=0 (n=19), B=10,000 Gibbs samples each, n0=1, k1=1
results.note: 28/10,000; quote line breaks; t-test p=0.0047 printed in text

results.claim: Parametric bootstrap for variance tau is more dispersed than even the k1=1 Bayes posterior, i.e. Bayes priors regularize
results.setup: Vasoconstriction y=1 group, n=20, Gibbs B=10,000, k1=1 or 9.5, start (116,554)
results.quote: Bayes techniques, even objective ones, have regularization effects that may

results.claim: Population-admixture MCMC on 197 individuals at 100 SNPs, J=3, recovers ethnic clusters unsupervised; burn-in 1000 then 2000 iterations
results.setup: 197 subjects, 100 SNPs, flat Dirichlet(1,1,1) and Beta(1,1) priors, Gibbs sampler (STRUCTURE)

limits: Impossible for any single prior to be uninformative for every parameter of interest t(theta)
Coverage-matching priors are not much used in practice
Objective Bayes is 'untethered': tenuous large-sample justification, unclear handling of stopping rules and selective inference
BIC sample size is ill-defined (prostate example); sample-size coherency is less convincing without priors from genuine experience
MCMC: not universal, favours convenient priors, successive draws correlated, no clear burn-in B0 or B, convergence factor unknown
Examples are small (n=39, n=20, 197 subjects); no timing or software details except STRUCTURE
Text layer drops minus signs and Greek symbols; equation details are unconfirmed
practices: Prefer a proper conjugate prior with small n0 (n0=1 popular) to keep the prior weakly informative (Sec 13.2)
Set x0 to xbar so posterior mean equals the MLE, or to a null value such as 0 (Sec 13.2)
Compare Bayes results with BCa/bootstrap as a check (Fig 13.3)
Check BIC against AIC and a Fisher-calibrated cn=1.92 (Sec 13.3, Fig 13.4)
Treat BIC as qualitative; do not put a fine point on it (Note 8)
Drop an initial burn-in B0 of MCMC draws and run B large enough that estimates settle (Sec 13.5)
Gibbs sampling: draw each coordinate from its full conditional, using conjugacy to get closed forms (Sec 13.4)
Any derived parameter t(theta) posterior comes directly from t(theta^(b)) of the draws (Sec 13.4)

terms.definition: g_{n0,x0}(mu)=c e^{n0[x0 alpha - psi(alpha)]}/V(mu); x0 is the average of n0 hypothetical prior observations
B(x)=f1(x)/f0(x); posterior odds ratio is prior odds ratio times the Bayes factor
BIC(M)=log f_thetahat(x) - (p/2) log(n); log B_BIC = BIC(M1)-BIC(M0)
M1 prior for sample size n is g1^(n)(mu)=sqrt(n) g1^(1)(sqrt(n) mu), spreading away from 0 at rate sqrt(n)
reduces multidimensional draws to univariate draws from full conditionals g_k(theta_k | theta_(-k), x)
p(i)Q(i,j)=p(j)Q(j,i); implies p is the chain's equilibrium distribution
initial B0 draws ignored before estimates are used
